n: Some time later, once the king’s anger cooled, he thought about Vashti and the decree he couldn’t undo. Between chapters 1 and 2 about four years pass, possibly while Xerxes was at war with Greece.
His attendants suggest a search for beautiful young women from which a new queen could be chosen.
Officials across the empire are to gather young women into the royal harem at Susa, under the care of Hegai. The women likely had little choice in the matter.
Whoever pleases the king most will become queen. The plan pleases him.

Now we meet Mordecai, a Jew living in Susa from the tribe of Benjamin. His ancestry includes Kish, the name of King Saul’s father — a link that becomes meaningful when Haman, descended from Saul’s old enemy Agag, appears.

f.g: A name related to the Babylonian god Marduk; Jews in exile often had local names.

n: His family (probably his great-grandfather Kish) had been deported from Jerusalem with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC.
Mordecai had raised his orphaned cousin Hadassah as his own daughter. Her Persian name, Esther, may mean “star.” Her loss and his kindness lay the groundwork for the story.

f.g: Possibly from Persian stara, “star,” or linked to the Babylonian goddess Ishtar.

n: Esther is taken into the palace along with many others. The text doesn’t say she volunteered; she is swept up in the king’s decree.
Esther wins Hegai’s favor. He gives her beauty treatments, special food, seven attendants, and the best rooms. Quietly, the pieces are falling into place.

f.g: Promoted her, gave her favored treatment.

n: On Mordecai’s instructions, Esther keeps her Jewish identity secret. This hidden fact will become the turning point of the story.
Every day Mordecai walks near the women’s court to check on her. His love and concern for Esther are steady and practical.
Each young woman underwent a full year of beauty treatments before her night with the king — six months with myrrh oil and six with perfumes.

f.g: A fragrant oil from tree resin, also among the gifts brought to the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:11).

n: When her turn came, each woman could take anything she wanted from the harem to impress the king.
After her night with the king, each woman moved to a second harem for concubines and might never see him again unless he asked for her by name. It was a lonely, uncertain life.
When Esther’s turn came, she asked only for what Hegai advised — showing humility and wisdom. Everyone who saw her admired her.

f.w: she required nothing but what Hegai
f.g: She trusted the counsel of the one who knew the king best.

n: Esther goes to the king in the winter of his seventh year, about 479 BC — four years after Vashti was removed.
The king loves Esther more than all the others and crowns her queen. An orphaned Jewish exile now sits beside the most powerful man on earth.

f.w: set the royal crown upon her head

n: The king celebrates with “Esther’s feast,” declares a holiday or tax relief for the provinces, and gives generous gifts.

f.g: Possibly a tax reduction, holiday, or release from labor.

n: Mordecai now holds a position “in the king’s gate,” where officials did business and judged cases — a sign he was a royal official.

f.g: The palace gatehouse, where court officials worked; archaeologists have found a large gatehouse at Susa.

f.w: the virgins were gathered together the second time
f.g: The meaning is unclear; perhaps a second gathering of women.

n: Esther still keeps her background secret and continues to honor Mordecai’s counsel, as she did growing up. Becoming queen did not make her proud.

f.w: like as when she was brought up with him

n: Two palace doorkeepers, angry at the king, plot to assassinate him. Such plots were real: Xerxes was eventually murdered by court officials.

f.g: Guarded the entrance — giving them dangerous access to the king.

n: Mordecai learns of the plot and tells Esther, who reports it to the king, giving Mordecai the credit.
The plot is confirmed and the traitors are executed. It is written in the royal records — but Mordecai receives no reward yet. This forgotten good deed will become crucial in chapter 6.

f.g: Probably impaled on a stake or pole, a Persian method of execution.
